The 1980 Wimbledon Championships arrived with Björn Borg as the defending champion and the chance to claim a fifth straight title on the London grass. The Swede had already won the event in each of the four previous editions, which made him the player to beat. Across the net stood John McEnroe, a younger player with an aggressive serve-and-volley game that stood out in an era when baseline play still dominated the tour.

From jeu de paume to lawn tennis: Wingfield's rules, the first Wimbledon in 1877 and the first national championships.

Tennis has a history that reaches back to the Middle Ages, when a game was played in northern France in which the ball was struck with the palm of the hand, which gave it the name jeu de paume. Over the centuries the game changed. The bare hand gave way to a glove and, by the 16th century, to a racket. What emerged was the game now called real tennis, played indoors in enclosed courts under intricate rules.

The event has taken place every year since 1877, from late June to mid-July, with breaks during both World Wars and in 2020 because of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Tennis is a racket sport played either one against one, in singles, or between two pairs, in doubles. Each player strikes a hollow rubber ball covered in felt with a strung racket, over or around the net and into the opponent’s court. Bobby Riggs had been one of the leading men's players of the 1940s. He finished the year ranked world number one three times, won six major titles including three at Wimbledon, and after leaving the professional circuit in 1951 he kept himself and tennis in the spotlight as a tireless promoter. In 1973, at 55, he claimed that the women's game was inferior and that he could still beat any of the top women. He first challenged Billie Jean King, who turned him down, and Margaret Court, then the world's top-ranked woman at 30, accepted instead.
